item.title: Osaka Sake & Izakaya Tasting: A Night of Drinking Osaka — Guide
item.description: Osaka takes drinking as seriously as eating, and a night in its izakaya and sake bars is one of the warmest experiences the city offers. The options run from tachinomi standing bars crammed under railway arches around Umeda and Namba, where a few hundred yen buys a glass and a skewer, to specialist sake bars pouring flights from breweries across the Kansai region and English-friendly guided tastings that walk you through junmai, ginjo and the differences between them.

item.title: Tebasaki: Nagoya's Peppery Glazed Chicken Wings — Guide
item.description: Tebasaki are Nagoya’s iconic chicken wings: fried crisp without batter, brushed while hot with a sweet-savoury tare glaze, then hit hard with white pepper, salt and sesame, producing a lacquered, peppery crunch that has made them the city’s definitive beer food. The style was born at the restaurant Furaibo in the 1960s, and its friendly rivalry with the cheekier chain Yamachan — whose wings bite back with even more pepper — divides the city into loyal camps that visitors are honour-bound to adjudicate over a cold beer.

item.title: Kokubuncho: Sendai's Neon-Lit Nightlife District — Guide
item.description: Kokubuncho is Tohoku’s largest entertainment district, a dense grid of neon-lit streets packed with izakaya (Japanese gastropubs), bars, karaoke boxes and restaurants a short walk from Sendai Station. By day it looks like an ordinary commercial street; by night, thousands of illuminated signs turn it into one of northern Japan’s liveliest nightlife scenes, popular with both locals winding down after work and visitors seeking a lively evening out. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aoba-ku, Sendai, Miyagi Hours Evening onward, busiest after 19:00 Admission Free to walk; drinks/food extra Time needed 2+ hours Best time Friday and Saturday nights What to See A dense grid of neon-lit izakaya, bars and karaoke boxes.

item.title: Awamori Guide: Okinawa's Spirit, Tasting & Izakaya
item.description: Awamori is Okinawa’s traditional distilled spirit and the oldest distilled liquor in Japan, with roots reaching back over 500 years to Ryukyu Kingdom trade. Made from long-grain Thai rice and black koji mould unique to Okinawa, it’s stronger and more characterful than mainland shochu. Aged versions, called kusu, mellow over years into something prized and complex. Sipping awamori at an izakaya — neat, on the rocks or in a highball — is one of the great pleasures of an Okinawan evening.

item.title: Osaka Solo Travel Guide: Counter Dining, Bar-Hopping & Day Trips
item.description: Osaka is arguably Japan’s best city for solo travel — not because it offers the solitary contemplation of Kyoto’s temples or Tokyo’s anonymous crowds, but because its food culture is fundamentally a solo-compatible architecture. The counter seat (kauntā) is the primary dining format; single-person tables are standard; standing bars assume you’ve arrived alone; and Osaka’s legendary directness means strangers begin conversations without the reserve you encounter in most Japanese cities. A solo traveller here is not an anomaly — they’re the default customer at most of the city’s best establishments.

item.title: Best Restaurants in Tokyo: Lunch & Dinner
item.description: Tokyo has more Michelin-starred restaurants than any other city on earth — including more starred sushi counters than the rest of the world combined. But the city’s real food culture runs far deeper than Michelin stars. This guide covers the best places to eat at every budget, from a ¥600 standing sushi bar to the counter where a master has been pressing rice for 40 years. 🍣 Sushi Standing Sushi Bars — The Tokyo Insider’s Lunch The best-value sushi experience in Tokyo isn’t an omakase counter — it’s a tachi-gui (standing) sushi bar in Tsukiji’s outer market or around major train stations.
